description: Our team is also representing the Collaborative Lab for Advancing Work in Space (CLAWS) from the University of Michigan. We have a group with a variety of skills in design, hardware, and development. We are excited to take part in this challenge!
summary:
Marswalk is a map and navigation tool for a proposed crewed mission to Jezero Crater. Astronauts would retrieve the Sapphire Canyon sample from Perseverance and collect samples at the Bright Angel to determine whether Mars once hosted life. In July 2024, Perseverance examined a rock there named Cheyava Falls, whose “leopard spots” NASA describes as a potential biosignature. Because Mars Sample Return is unfunded, the Sapphire Canyon sample has no planned route to Earth and remains unanalyzed.

Earth-Mars signal delay reaches about 22 minutes each way, so Mission Control cannot guide a spacewalk in real time. Marswalk helps equips the crew to decide independently. Inside a Mars-capable pressurized rover or habitat, astronauts use an interactive laptop or tablet map combining USGS HiRISE terrain, HRSC color imagery, CRISM mineral maps, THEMIS thermal inertia and Perseverance images into a single walk-scale view. Astronauts can plan a route that avoids slopes steeper than 20°, review walk times and oxygen use, and follow the route in a first-person visor view. During the EVA, the map is seen in an AR heads-up display in the helmet visor, currently simulated in a browser. A safe-return boundary shrinks as oxygen is consumed, showing the crew how far they can travel and still reach the rover. Tested against Perseverance’s actual 12.4 km traverse, only 0.3% of the path crosses terrain flagged as too steep.
details:
Marswalk is designed for a proposed crewed mission to Jezero Crater, in which astronauts and an unpressurized rover travel to Bright Angel to retrieve the Sapphire Canyon sample from Perseverance and collect additional samples, in order to determine whether the “leopard spots” at Cheyava Falls were produced by life. The tool operates in two modes. In plan mode, used inside a pressurized rover, the crew clicks waypoints and the route steers around slopes steeper than 20°, while the display reports walk time, oxygen used and oxygen remaining on arrival. Terrain, natural color, and CRISM mineral and THEMIS thermal layers can be switched on a single map. In walk mode, the plan becomes a first-person visor view at a height of 1.7 m, with a compass pointing to the rover and a minimap. A safe-return boundary shows every location the crew can reach and still return from with a 30-minute oxygen reserve. The boundary shrinks as oxygen is consumed, turning yellow and then red.

Signal delay between Earth and Mars reaches about 22 minutes each way, so Mission Control cannot guide a spacewalk in real time. Marswalk allows the crew to see how far they can travel and still return, without waiting for direct instructions from Earth. Flight planners receive a single view of route, time, oxygen and hazards, scientists receive sample targets placed on real terrain, and students and the public can walk Bright Angel in a web browser. The intended impact is safer travel, faster planning and more science per spacewalk.

The application was built with React, TypeScript and Vite, and uses Three.js for the 3D and visor views. A tested logic engine runs Dijkstra’s algorithm over a 5 m slope grid and traces the safe-return boundary with marching squares. A Python pipeline builds the slope, basemap, color, mineral and thermal layers from USGS HiRISE terrain and orthomosaics, HRSC color (ESA/DLR/FU Berlin), CRISM minerals, THEMIS thermal inertia and Perseverance images. The tool runs in a browser without special hardware, and the visor view is designed for later use on an AR headset. Claude (Anthropic) was used for coding, debugging, research and writing assistance.

Most Mars maps show terrain. Marswalk instead shows how far a crew can go and still get back, an answer that is dependent on resource consumption such as oxygen levels. The same plan carries from the pressurized rover display to the visor view. We also checked the route logic against Perseverance’s actual 12.4 km traverse, and only 0.3% of that path crosses ground we flagged as too steep.

Several factors shaped this design. We chose Bright Angel because it holds the strongest lead on ancient life on Mars and has the data a walking route requires, including 1 m elevation, 25 cm imagery and rover photographs. The 20° slope limit is our own assumption based on safe oxygen consumption as astronauts navigate higher slopes, and the safe-return boundary uses a 30-minute oxygen reserve. The mission assumes a pair of astronauts and a pressurized rover, with an EVA of 6 hours nominal and 8 hours maximum. The data layers differ in resolution (5 m slope, 2 m base map, 18 to 36 m minerals, about 50 m color and about 100 m thermal), and the application labels each one. The terrain, slope, imagery, mineral and thermal layers and the Cheyava Falls location are real. The rover position, sample points, hazards, oxygen and speed constants, and dust-devil window are notional. East-west distances run about 5% long because of the source map projection. Future work includes real suit physiology, separate uphill and downhill costs, rover-camera 3D terrain, and the visor view on an AR headset.
